claims.text: Black presents the Heptaplus as containing a theory of allegory that departs from mainstream medieval and Renaissance exegesis and is tied to contemporary debate on the nature and action of the intellect.

quotes.text: This is a study in the history of allegory. It focuses on a particular theory of allegory, developed by the Italian philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his Heptaplus (1489), a sevenfold commentary on the account of the six days of creation contained in Genesis 1. This theory, which differs in a number of ways from mainstream medieval and Renaissance thinking on biblical exegesis, is connected to a philosophical issue which was the subject of considerable debate at the time: the nature and action of the intellect.

judged.justification: Frames the Heptaplus through the intellect debate rather than only as cosmology.

claims.text: Black argues that the theory of allegory of the second proem derives largely from the Neoplatonic tradition, especially the Dionysian corpus, and that the parallels with Pseudo-Dionysius lead to the question of intellectual ascent (anagogy).

quotes.text: His theory of allegory is derived largely from the Neoplatonic tradition and particularly, I argue, from this tradition's Christian incarnation in the works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite. The parallels between Pico and Pseudo-Dionysius lead to a consideration of epistemology, specifically in relation to the idea of intellectual ascent or 'anagogy' (to use Dionysius's term).

judged.justification: Makes Dionysius the source of Heptaplus hermeneutics, not only of its angel-lore.

claims.text: The first proem justifies a hidden non-literal meaning in the Bible, and its argument rests on a semiotic and social distinction between esoteric and exoteric meaning.

quotes.text: In the first proem he provides an overall justification for there being a hidden non-literal meaning in the Bible in general and the Genesis account in particular. His argument hinges on a semiotic and social distinction between esoteric and exoteric meaning.

claims.text: Black proposes that the Heptaplus should be viewed as an expression of the role of the intellect in man's progress to felicitas.

quotes.text: I propose that the Heptaplus should be viewed as an expression of the role of the intellect in man's progress to felicitas.

judged.justification: Offers an organising reading of the whole work.

claims.text: Black argues that the seven-fold structure of the Heptaplus reflects the forty-nine gates of understanding through which, according to texts Pico read, Moses ascended and whose knowledge he concealed in the Genesis account.

quotes.text: the structure of the work as a whole, which is based on the number seven (symbolizing the sabbath). In conclusion, I argue that this structure reflects the forty-nine gates of understanding through which, according to texts read by Pico, Moses ascended, and knowledge of which he concealed in the Genesis account.

judged.justification: Reads the sevenfold architecture as an image of ascent, not only of sabbath.

claims.text: Black holds that Pico's engagement with the debate on the intellect was influenced by the Jewish tradition, in its application to hermeneutics rather than in the details of epistemology.

quotes.text: Pico's engagement with this matter was influenced by the Jewish tradition, not so much in the details of his epistemology as in his manner of applying it to hermeneutics.

claims.text: In Florence Pico made the acquaintance of Poliziano, Benivieni and Ficino among others, and around this time took up the project of reconciling Plato and Aristotle.

quotes.text: He then spent some time in Florence, making the acquaintance of several prominent humanists, writers and philosophers, including Angelo Poliziano, Girolamo Benivieni and Marsilio Ficino. It appears to be around this time that he became interested in what was to become a lifelong project: the reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle.

bears_on.note: First acquaintance in Florence.
First acquaintance in Florence.
First acquaintance in Florence, roughly when the concord project began.

claims.text: The lifelong reconciliation project never took written form as such; De ente et uno represents a part of it and the Conclusiones give intimations of the intended method.

quotes.text: It appears to be around this time that he became interested in what was to become a lifelong project: the reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle.
This never saw written form as such, although a part of it is represented by De ente et uno (Garin, 386-441). Intimations of Pico's intended method also appear in the Conclusiones.

claims.text: The Commento, written around 1485-1486, is a commentary strongly influenced by Platonism and Neoplatonism on a love poem by Benivieni that is itself based on Ficino's commentary on Plato's Symposium.

quotes.text: his earliest major work, written around 1485-1486, the Commento sopra una canzone d'amore. This is a commentary, strongly influenced by Platonism and Neoplatonism, on a love poem by Benivieni, itself based on Ficino's commentary on Plato's Symposium.

bears_on.note: Pico's Commento glosses Benivieni's poem.
The poem rests on Ficino's Symposium commentary.

claims.text: Black says Ficino's interpretation of Plato was tendentious: he wished to establish Platonism as the philosophy of choice for Christians against a scholastic Aristotelianism he thought mired in heresy about the soul.

quotes.text: Ficino's interpretation of Plato and Platonism was tendentious. He wished to establish it as the philosophy of choice for Christians, in comparison with scholastic Aristotelianism, which was (in his view) mired in the heresies of Alexander of Aphrodisias and Averroes regarding the soul and immortality.

bears_on.note: Ficino's partisan Platonism sets the contrast with Pico's concord project.

judged.justification: Sets Ficino as partisan against Pico's less partisan stance.

claims.text: Black says Pico's own position was less partisan than Ficino's, as seen in his reply of 9 June 1485 to Barbaro's attack on scholastic barbarism, defending scholasticism on the ground that truth alone matters.

quotes.text: Ficino's interpretation of Plato and Platonism was tendentious.

Pico's own position was less partisan, as we can see from his response to one such attack, made by his friend Ermolao Barbaro in a letter to Pico of April 1485. In his reply, from Florence, dated 9 June 1485, Pico formulated a defence of scholasticism, arguing that the truth was the only thing of consequence, regardless of the manner in which it was expressed.

bears_on.note: Barbaro (called Pico's friend) attacked scholastic Latin; Pico replied in 1485.
Pico's stance is contrasted with Ficino's partisanship.

claims.text: Black sees no reason to doubt Pico's sincerity in the earlier defence of scholasticism, since Pico followed that path in practice, having spent time among the Averroists of Padua and then going to Paris.

quotes.text: There seems little reason to doubt the sincerity of this

argument, even though it is put in the mouth of a barbaric medieval philosopher, since Pico followed this path in practice as well as in theory. He had previously spent time among the Averroists of Padua; and soon after writing this letter, he went to study in Paris

claims.hedge_words: There seems little reason to doubt

bears_on.note: Sincerity of the reply to Barbaro's letter.

claims.text: Pico planned to debate nine hundred conclusions in Rome in the manner of Parisian disputation, and published them on 7 November.

quotes.text: In March 1486 he returned to Florence. His next project, in line with his recent experience, was conceived after the style of 'Parisian' disputation. He proposed to hold a public debate in Rome on nine hundred 'conclusions' or 'theses'
He then moved to Rome in the autumn of that year and published them on 7 November.

claims.text: Black describes the Conclusiones as formally far from the Heptaplus: a miscellaneous collection of bare bones that, despite commentators' efforts, do not form a coherent body.

quotes.text: The Conclusiones are formally as far removed from the Heptaplus as can be imagined. While the later text exhibits a complete and perfected structure, the earlier one is a miscellaneous collection of bare bones, which do not, despite the best efforts of ingenious commentators, form a single skeleton, let alone a coherent body.

judged.justification: Contrasts with readings that seek a single system in the 900.

claims.text: A papal committee scrutinised the Conclusiones for several months and found fault first with seven, then thirteen of them; the debate never took place, so Pico's position on most of them is unknown.

quotes.text: They were intended to be debated, following the scholastic method of quaestiones; but we do not know what position Pico would have taken on most of them, because the debate never took place. Instead there followed several months of scrutiny and disputation by a papal committee, which found fault first with seven, then thirteen of the nine hundred Conclusiones.

open_questions.text: Pico's position on most of the theses is unknown because the debate did not occur.

basis_quote.text: we do not know what position Pico would have taken on most of them, because the debate never took place

bears_on.note: Papal committee censure of seven then thirteen theses.

claims.text: Pico's Apologia responded to the censure as a preamble to the debate and a defence of the thirteen condemned propositions, blaming the committee for misreading his words.

quotes.text: Pico's response to this censure was the Apologia, which serves as both an explanatory preamble to his proposed debate, and a defence of the thirteen condemned propositions. The charge of heterodoxy, he complained, resulted from the failure of the examining committee to interpret the meanings of his words correctly.

bears_on.note: Pico's defence complains the committee misread him.

claims.text: Innocent VIII issued a bull dated 8 August 1487 banning the book, not promulgated until 15 December; by then Pico had fled toward Paris and been captured and arrested on the way.

quotes.text: Innocent VIII issued a bull, dated 8 August 1487, banning the book's dissemination. This was not actually promulgated until 15 December, however, and by this time Pico had fled to Paris; on the way he was captured and arrested.

bears_on.note: Bull banning the Conclusiones.

claims.text: Lorenzo de' Medici helped secure Pico's release and offered him hospitality in Florence; Black reads this as a pragmatic solution keeping Pico's doctrines within Florentine libraries and Lorenzo's circle.

quotes.text: His release was secured with the assistance of Lorenzo de' Medici, who offered him hospitality in Florence.

One can see this as a pragmatic solution to a potentially embarrassing situation: Pico was kept out of Rome and his 'unsound' doctrines were confined to the rarefied atmosphere of Florentine libraries and the group of intellectuals who gathered around Lorenzo.

bears_on.note: Lorenzo secured release and gave hospitality.

claims.text: Black says the Roman affair produced the Conclusiones, the Apologia and the Oratio, and that the Oratio is essentially a version of the first part of the Apologia presented as an introductory speech to the debate.

quotes.text: The Roman affair, then, produced a group of three works: the Conclusiones themselves, the Apologia, and the Oratio, now commonly subtitled 'On the Dignity of Man'. This last is essentially a version of the first part of the Apologia, presenting itself as an introductory speech to the proposed disputation.

claims.text: Black notes that Copenhaver argues the subtitle 'On the Dignity of Man' misrepresents the work's content.

quotes.text: B.P. Copenhaver, 'The Secret of Pico's Oration: Cabala and Renaissance Philosophy', Midwest Studies in Philosophy, 26 (2002), 56-81, argues that the subtitle 'On the Dignity of Man' is a misrepresentation of the work's content.

claims.text: After returning to Florence Pico turned to biblical commentary, the pre-eminent result being the Heptaplus, contemporary with an incomplete series of Psalm commentaries begun in 1488.

quotes.text: In the period directly following his return to Florence, Pico turned his attention to biblical commentary. The pre-eminent result of this is the Heptaplus
Contemporary with it is an incomplete series of commentaries on the Psalms, begun in 1488 and continued over the next couple of years.

claims.text: Lorenzo wrote in June 1489 that Pico lived like a monk in theological work; Black reads the letter as an effort at rehabilitation, which failed, since Lanfredini reported that the pope found Pico's theology intolerable and preferred poetry.

quotes.text: On 13 June 1489, Lorenzo de' Medici wrote to his ambassador in Rome, Giovanni Lanfredini, saying: Pico lives like a monk, he is constantly engaged in theological work

The letter reads like an effort towards rehabilitation. It was unsuccessful, as a subsequent letter from Lanfredini attests: the pope finds Pico's continuing interest in theology intolerable and would prefer him to write poetry.

bears_on.note: Lorenzo's letter defends Pico's theological work.
The pope's reported view of Pico's theology.

claims.text: Black says that as far as the pope was concerned the Heptaplus continued the heretical tendencies of the Conclusiones, and that Lorenzo again defended Pico's work; several intellectuals, including Barbaro, wrote to admire it.

quotes.text: As far as the pope was concerned, the Heptaplus was a continuation of the heretical tendencies Pico had displayed in the Conclusiones. Lorenzo, however, once again defended Pico's work

was enthusiastically received by a number of intellectuals and humanists. Several wrote to express their admiration: these included Matteo Vero, Gerolamo Donato, Cristoforo Landino, Bartolomeo Fontio and Ermolao Barbaro, among others.

bears_on.note: Papal view of the Heptaplus.
Lorenzo defended the Heptaplus.
Barbaro among those who wrote to admire the Heptaplus.

claims.text: De ente et uno, published in 1490, is all Pico managed to write of his proposed Concordia Platonis et Aristotelis.

quotes.text: The Heptaplus was Pico's last completed work. In 1490 he published a brief tract entitled De ente et uno, which is all he managed
to write of his proposed Concordia Platonis et Aristotelis

judged.justification: Treats the concord as a project realised only in a short tract.

claims.text: Gianfrancesco Pico's Vita stresses Pico's orthodoxy and holiness, dismisses the Roman affair as youthful folly, and largely overlooks his interest in kabbalah.

quotes.text: Gianfrancesco's Vita emphasizes Pico's orthodoxy and holiness. The events of the Roman affair are dismissed as a youthful folly, equated with his early pursuit of women, from which he turned away to embrace a life of quiet sanctity and scholarship.
Likewise, Pico's interest in kabbalah one of the factors in the Conclusiones scandal is largely overlooked.

bears_on.note: The nephew's Vita, per Black, downplays Pico's kabbalah and the Roman affair.

judged.justification: Warns that the earliest biography is an apologetic source on kabbalah.

claims.text: Black says the Hebrew literary tradition presented Pico with both biblical exegesis and philosophy, and was one of his points of entry into the Arabic tradition, notably through otherwise untranslated works of or on Averroes.

quotes.text: The Hebrew literary tradition presented Pico with works of biblical exegesis and with works of philosophy; in the latter case, it represented one of his points of entry into the Arabic tradition as well, especially through several otherwise untranslated works of or on Averroes.

claims.text: Black names three scholars who made Jewish and Arabic works available to Pico, orally or textually: Elijah Delmedigo, Flavius Mithridates and Johanan Alemanno.

quotes.text: Three scholars in particular played an important role in making works from the Jewish and Arabic traditions available to Pico, either orally or textually, and, if textually, either in Hebrew or in Latin translations. These are Elijah Delmedigo, Flavius Mithridates and Jo.hanan Alemanno.

bears_on.note: Mithridates as one of three mediators of Jewish and Arabic works to Pico.

claims.text: Delmedigo's two treatises on the intellect were first composed in Latin at Pico's request, and the original Latin versions are not extant, so the surviving Hebrew versions cannot be a sure guide to what he wrote for Pico.

quotes.text: The two treatises on the intellect were initially composed in Latin at Pico's request; Delmedigo himself then translated them into Hebrew
The original Latin versions are not extant.
We cannot, therefore, use the Hebrew versions of the treatises on the intellect as a sure guide to what Delmedigo originally wrote for Pico.

open_questions.text: What Delmedigo wrote in Latin for Pico on the intellect is unrecoverable from the extant Hebrew versions.

basis_quote.text: We cannot, therefore, use the Hebrew versions of the treatises on the intellect as a sure guide to what Delmedigo originally wrote for Pico.

claims.text: Black reports that Delmedigo, in a long letter to Pico, gives bibliographies of writers said to help prove that the first principle is separate from matter, a doctrine he says they received by revelation and which must therefore be believed.

quotes.text: We also possess a lengthy letter from Delmedigo to Pico, which is particularly interesting from our current perspective because it casts some light on Pico's literary research and includes three bibliographies. According to Delmedigo, the bibliographies constitute a list of writers who will help to prove that the first principle is separate from matter; they support what Aristotle said, but they support this doctrine having received it 'by revelation' and therefore must be believed.

claims.text: Delmedigo's letter to Pico lists under 'Kabbalah' the Zohar, a work by Recanati, Gikatilla's Sha'arei orah, and other works, adding that he cannot recall further names.

quotes.text: The right-hand column contains a list entitled 'Kabbalah': Delmedigo notes the existence of the Zohar, the Me'irat einayim (probably referring to a commentary on Nahmanides by Isaac of Acre, late-thirteenth to mid-fourteenth centuries), the Sha'arei orah of Joseph Gikatilla (1248 - c. 1325), Recanati, the Ma'arekhet ha-elohut

claims.text: Black argues that Delmedigo's letter to Pico, addressed to him in Rome, must date from late November 1486 at the earliest, and that it shows Pico's kabbalah studies already well under way.

quotes.text: The letter is undated. It is, however, addressed to Pico in Rome, and must therefore have been written in late November 1486 at the earliest. As Delmedigo himself observes in the letter, Pico's studies of kabbalah were already well underway.

claims.text: Black reports it has been demonstrated (citing Wirszubski) that Mithridates's translation of Recanati's Pentateuch commentary was the single most influential source for Pico's interpretation of kabbalah in the Conclusiones, so Pico had read it before November 1486.

quotes.text: By 'Ricanato' he means the kabbalist Menahem Recanati (late thirteenth-early fourteenth centuries), two of whose works were translated for Pico by Flavius Mithridates (see below): the commentary on the Pentateuch and the commentary on prayers.

It has been demonstrated that this work was the single most influential source for Pico's interpretation of kabbalah in the Conclusiones. Pico had therefore read it before these were completed in November 1486 and before Delmedigo wrote this letter.
Wirszubski, Pico's Encounter, 53-56. 49 See Flavius Mithridates, Sermo de passione Domini

bears_on.note: Mithridates translated the work that most influenced Pico's kabbalah.

judged.justification: Names the dominant kabbalistic source of the 900.

claims.text: The lost Latin translation of Recanati's Pentateuch commentary cannot be shown to have been sent by Delmedigo, since no volume of Recanati is identifiable in Pico's library inventory.

quotes.text: No volume of Recanati is identifiable in Pico's library inventory. We cannot, for this reason, be sure that Delmedigo ever sent this book or that, if he did, it was indeed the commentary on the Pentateuch.

claims.hedge_words: We cannot, for this reason, be sure

open_questions.text: Whether Delmedigo sent Pico a Recanati volume, and which one, is undetermined.

basis_quote.text: We cannot, for this reason, be sure that Delmedigo ever sent this book

claims.text: Black says Delmedigo was not involved with biblical exegesis, unlike Mithridates and Alemanno, but was a conduit for Averroes and important to Pico's Hebrew studies.

quotes.text: Unlike Mithridates and Alemanno, Delmedigo was not involved with matters of biblical exegesis. His role in Pico's Hebrew studies, however, was by no means negligible; and he has further importance as a conduit for the thought of Averroes.

bears_on.note: Contrast with Mithridates as exegetical source.

claims.text: Around 1486 Mithridates translated for Pico a substantial corpus of Hebrew texts into Latin, of which the surviving part amounts to over 3,500 pages in five Vatican manuscripts.

quotes.text: Documentation of their working relationship begins in 1486. Around this time, as has already been mentioned, Mithridates translated a substantial corpus of Hebrew texts into Latin specifically for Pico. Some of these are no longer extant. What survives, in five manuscripts held in the Vatican library, amounts to over 3,500 pages.

bears_on.note: Translation corpus made for Pico.

claims.text: Links between the translations and the Conclusiones show that part of the corpus, certainly Vat. Ebr. 190 and the lost Recanati manuscript, had been completed and read by Pico by November 1486, while Vat. Ebr. 189 postdates it.

quotes.text: Links between these translated texts and Pico's own Conclusiones demonstrate that a proportion of the translations, and certainly those contained in Vat. Ebr. 190 as well as the lost Recanati manuscript mentioned above, had been completed (and read by Pico) by November 1486.
On the other hand, evidence from marginal notes made by Mithridates shows that Vat. Ebr. 189 postdates this.

bears_on.note: Dating of Mithridates's translations against the Conclusiones.

claims.text: The translated corpus omits the Sefer Ye.zirah and the Zohar, but Pico knew they existed.

quotes.text: it omits two kabbalistic texts of central importance, the Sefer Ye.zirah and the Zohar. Pico was nonetheless aware of their existence

claims.text: Black says the translated corpus includes more than one strand of kabbalah, but Pico understood kabbalah as handed down orally from Moses, so the places and dates of composition mattered little to him.

quotes.text: The translated corpus includes more than one strand of kabbalah. We have no reason to believe that any such perspective was available or of interest to Pico. His understanding was that the kabbalah had been handed down orally from Moses: the places and dates of composition of these texts were therefore of relative unimportance.

judged.justification: Explains why Pico does not distinguish kabbalistic schools or dates.

claims.text: Marginal markings in the translated manuscripts against passages used, sometimes almost verbatim, in the Conclusiones show that Pico read, marked and reused them; Black adds that several concern exegesis and are potentially important background to the Heptaplus.

quotes.text: These manuscripts are the single most significant channel through which Hebrew thought, specifically kabbalah, was made available to Pico. The many instances of marginal markings (a vertical line surmounted by two dots) against sections of these manuscripts which were used, sometimes almost verbatim, in the Conclusiones provide evidence that Pico read these texts, marked passages of interest and then reused them in his own works.
Several of these texts are concerned with matters of biblical exegesis, and they should therefore be considered as potentially important background material for the Heptaplus.

bears_on.note: Mithridates's manuscripts are the main channel of kabbalah to Pico.

judged.justification: Links the Mithridates corpus to the Heptaplus as well as the 900.

claims.text: Mithridates's translations contain interpolations: some clarify letter-number passages, some add a Christian veneer, and some add references to kabbalah and kabbalists absent from the original.

quotes.text: the other notable feature of these translations is that Mithridates introduced a number of interpolations of several different sorts. Some were evidently intended to make difficult passages (particularly those involving letters treated as numbers) more comprehensible to Pico; others lent a Christian veneer to the Jewish sources; and still others

bears_on.note: Mithridates altered his sources for Pico.

judged.justification: Pico's kabbalistic sources reached him already Christianised.

claims.text: Pico's association with Mithridates apparently ended before March 1489 for reasons that remain unclear.

quotes.text: Some time before March 1489, Pico's association with Mithridates apparently came to an end, for reasons that remain unclear.

open_questions.text: Why Pico's association with Mithridates ended is unknown.

bears_on.note: End of their working relationship.

claims.text: Around 1488 Pico met the Jewish scholar Alemanno, whose Song of Songs commentary was written apparently at Pico's request and who was composing a Genesis commentary at about the time of the Heptaplus.

quotes.text: Around 1488 Pico made the acquaintance of another Jewish scholar, Johanan Alemanno

He wrote a long commentary on the Song of Songs, apparently (he says in the introduction) after a request from Pico. Furthermore, at around the same time that Pico was working on the Heptaplus, Alemanno was composing his own Genesis commentary, the Einei ha-edah

judged.justification: A contemporary Genesis commentary in Pico's circle.

claims.text: Black finds a shared interest of Alemanno and Pico in exegesis and intellectual ascent easy to make out but concrete links between their texts hard to show, and there is no evidence that Pico read the Einei ha-edah.

quotes.text: The point that Alemanno and Pico had a common interest in biblical exegesis and the idea of intellectual ascent is easily made. It is harder to demonstrate any concrete links between the texts of the two writers. Temporal coincidence notwithstanding, we have no evidence that Pico read (or had read to him) the Einei ha-edah.

open_questions.text: Whether Pico knew Alemanno's Genesis commentary is unattested.

basis_quote.text: we have no evidence that Pico read (or had read to him) the Einei ha-edah

claims.text: Black cautions against taking literally, given epistolary convention, Pico's attribution of his interest in Genesis to Lorenzo de' Medici in the Heptaplus introduction (and Alemanno's attribution of his commentary to Pico).

quotes.text: Equally, given the rhetorical conventions of an introductory epistle, it might be unwise to put too much weight on Alemanno's attribution of his writing of the Song of Songs commentary to Pico; just as, in the introduction to the Heptaplus, we need not necessarily take literally Pico's attribution of his interest in Genesis to Lorenzo de' Medici.

bears_on.note: Lorenzo as dedicatee and stated stimulus of the Heptaplus.

claims.text: Black says information probably passed between Pico and Alemanno in conversation, so Alemanno may have introduced other works and broadened Pico's grasp of the textual bases of doctrines Mithridates had introduced.

quotes.text: we must bear in mind the likelihood that information passed between Pico and Alemanno in conversation. We should therefore reckon with the possibility that Alemanno introduced other works to Pico and broadened his understanding of the textual bases of the doctrines to which Mithridates had already introduced him.

bears_on.note: Alemanno widens what Mithridates provided.

claims.text: Pico accumulated a sizeable collection of Hebrew books not represented in the translated corpus and used some in his biblical commentaries, though the details are obscure.

quotes.text: His knowledge of this tradition does not appear to have been based solely on translations and oral contact, however, since he accumulated a sizeable collection of Hebrew books and manuscripts which were not represented in the translated corpus. He made use of some of these books in his biblical commentaries. Although this much is clear, the details recede into obscurity.

open_questions.text: Which untranslated Hebrew books Pico used is unclear.

basis_quote.text: Although this much is clear, the details recede into obscurity.

claims.text: Pico replied to a letter from Ficino of 8 September 1486, writing that he had spent a whole month at Hebrew day and night and could now compose a letter not yet worthy of praise but without fault; Black says how much Hebrew this was is hard to say.

quotes.text: In a letter written in reply to one sent by Ficino on 8 September 1486, and probably not itself composed before 15 October of the same year, Pico wrote that he had spent the whole month studying Hebrew day and night, and that his command of it was now sufficient to compose a letter 'not yet, indeed, worthy of praise, but without
fault'. But quite how much Hebrew this was is hard to say.

bears_on.note: Pico's 1486 reply to Ficino reports his Hebrew study.

claims.text: Black argues that the Psalm expositions show Pico had enough Hebrew to draw on commentators for individual words in philological sections, but this does not necessarily imply he could read whole treatises by Recanati, Abulafia, Gikatilla or Alemanno.

quotes.text: The Expositiones in Psalmos demonstrate that Pico had sufficient knowledge of Hebrew to draw material from these commentators, as well as to indicate instances in which the Latin or Greek text departed from the Hebrew.
This level of interest and knowledge does not necessarily imply the ability to read entire treatises by such writers as Recanati, Abulafia, Gikatilla and Alemanno, however.

judged.justification: Limits how directly Pico could have known the Hebrew kabbalistic sources.

claims.text: Black hypothesises that Pico and Mithridates jointly began translating Job through Gersonides, with Mithridates continuing in Pico's absence after chapter 10, and that the manuscript reflects a teacher-pupil relationship.

quotes.text: In effect, my hypothesis is that Pico and Mithridates jointly embarked on the project of translating Job via Gersonides and that after they had reached the end of chapter 10, Mithridates continued in Pico's absence, subsequently giving the completed text to him, at which point Pico added further annotations throughout the second section.
The manuscript appears very much to be the product of a teacher-pupil relationship.

bears_on.note: Black reads the Job manuscript as the product of a teacher-pupil relationship.

claims.text: Black argues that the unusual Jewish exegetical terminology in Pico's Apologia, matching Bahya ben Asher, reached Pico by oral transmission from Mithridates or another Jewish associate, since the note in Pico's hand is in a manuscript of another work that does not contain it.

quotes.text: An example is Pico's discussion of Jewish exegetical terminology in the Apologia. The terminology he uses is atypical of medieval Jewish exegesis and has a distinct source in the work of the biblical commentator Bahya ben Asher (thirteenth century)
Since it does not derive from this work, it seems likely that this note reflects the oral transmission of information from Mithridates (or another Jewish associate) to Pico.

bears_on.note: Oral transmission from Mithridates as the probable channel.

claims.text: Black warns that oral contact cannot be assumed to be a full conduit: information would not necessarily have been shared fully, Mithridates distorted texts in a Christianizing manner, and Delmedigo deliberately withheld information about kabbalah from works produced for Pico, who was his patron.

quotes.text: On the other hand, we cannot simply assume oral contact as a conduit for everything. We should remember that information would not necessarily have been shared fully or without ulterior motive. I have already mentioned the interpolations made by Mithridates, which in some cases distorted Hebrew texts in a Christianizing manner.

In the case of Delmedigo, we have concrete evidence that he at certain points deliberately withheld information about kabbalah from works he produced for Pico. Pico acted as patron to Delmedigo and Alemanno

bears_on.note: Mithridates's Christianising interpolations limit what Pico could learn.

judged.justification: Qualifies confident reconstructions of Pico's Jewish learning.

claims.text: Black concludes that, given the limits of the evidence, one cannot assume Pico could read complete kabbalistic treatises unaided even in 1489; he was a pioneer in his area of interest, kabbalah, rather than in linguistic ability, and approached it through the translated corpus and oral contact.

quotes.text: On balance, given these limitations, we cannot assume that, even in 1489, he would have been able to read complete kabbalistic treatises unaided

While I by no means wish to rob Pico of his status as a pioneer among Christian Hebraists, I believe that he is a pioneer in his particular area of interest kabbalah rather than in his linguistic ability; and this area of interest he approached first and foremost through the translated corpus and oral contact.

judged.justification: Sets the methodological limit on attributing Hebrew-text knowledge to Pico.

claims.text: Black states that he generally seeks the origins of Jewish influence on the Heptaplus in works known to be available to Pico in Latin, printed or in Mithridates's corpus, while citing Alemanno and Delmedigo as evidence of contemporary Jewish thought in Pico's circle.

quotes.text: This conclusion has provided the methodological basis for my analysis of the role of Jewish sources in Pico's works. I hope to demonstrate that Pico's interest in this material had an important influence on the Heptaplus; but I have generally sought to locate the origins of this influence in works which we know were available to him in Latin, whether through printed editions or Mithridates's corpus of translations.

I have, nonetheless, referred in several instances to Hebrew works by Alemanno and Delmedigo, as these provide evidence of contemporary Jewish thought in a circle to which we know Pico had a certain proximity.

claims.text: The Heptaplus is titled as a sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis for Lorenzo de' Medici; Roberto Salviati saw it into print at his own expense in a dedicatory epistle calling the subject physical and divine mysteries.

quotes.text: The full title is 'Heptaplus: On the Sevenfold Narration of the Six Days of Genesis, for Lorenzo de' Medici'. In a brief dedicatory epistle, Roberto Salviati, the Florentine humanist who undertook the printing and distribution of the work, describes these 'first fruits' of Pico as 'most excellent, not just in my judgement, but in the judgement of everyone'; for this reason, he has printed an 'accurate impression' at his own expense. The subject of the book, according to Salviati, is 'physical and divine mysteries'.

bears_on.note: The Heptaplus is dedicated to Lorenzo.

claims.text: Black suggests that describing the Heptaplus as Pico's first fruits perhaps shows a deliberate wish to overlook the recent scandal.

quotes.text: The description of the Heptaplus as representing the 'first fruits' of Pico's studies perhaps betrays a deliberate desire to overlook the recent scandal.

bears_on.note: The dedicatory epistle may avoid the 1487 scandal.

claims.text: Black summarises the first proem as mostly a justification, by pagan and Christian examples, of an esoteric reading of the Bible distinguishing literal 'shell' from non-literal 'kernel', with the claim that the secrets of the whole of nature lie in the six days.

quotes.text: most of the first proem consists of a justification, via ancient pagan and Christian examples, of an esoteric reading of the Bible: that is, of the distinction between literal and non-literal reading, or, as Pico calls it, the 'shell' and 'kernel'. His essential claim is that the 'secrets of the whole of nature' are contained in the narrative of the six days of creation.

claims.text: Black summarises the second proem as describing a theory of allegory related to a cosmic model of three worlds, the sublunary, the celestial and the angelic or intellectual, each of the seven expositions except the last treating an aspect of these worlds separately or in combination, in seven chapters each.

quotes.text: The second proem describes his theory of allegory. It is related to a cosmic model according to which the created universe is composed of three worlds: the sublunary, the celestial and the angelic or intellectual. Each of the seven expositions (with the exception of the last, which discusses
man's felicitas) will address an aspect of these worlds: either separately or in combination. Each of these expositions, in turn, is to have seven chapters.

judged.justification: Gives the architecture needed to place the angelic world: one of three worlds, treated separately in the third exposition and in combination elsewhere.

claims.text: The Genesis text quoted after the proems runs from verse 1 to verse 27 in the Vulgate, ending with the creation of man on the sixth day and omitting the seventh day of Genesis 2.1.

quotes.text: There follows a quotation of the opening of the first chapter of Genesis, from verse 1 to verse 27, in the Latin of the Vulgate. It is this extract of the text that I shall refer to throughout this study as the Genesis narrative. Note that it finishes with the creation of man on the sixth day, and does not include the account of the seventh day, which is to be found in Genesis 2.1.

claims.text: At the start of each exposition Pico defines a body of knowledge, such as Aristotelian physics or the angelic metaphysics of Pseudo-Dionysius, and then derives information about it from the Genesis narrative by allegorical reading.

quotes.text: At the start of each exposition Pico defines a certain body of knowledge: Aristotelian physics, for example, or the angelic metaphysics of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. He then proceeds to derive information concerning this body of knowledge from the Genesis narrative, by a process of allegorical reading.

judged.justification: States the working principle: the Genesis text is constant and the framework, including Dionysian angelic metaphysics, is imposed by definition and read into it.

claims.text: The frame of reference of the first exposition is natural philosophy and the world of generation and corruption; it opens with the doctrines of natural philosophers, not with the Bible.

quotes.text: The frame of reference of the first exposition is natural philosophy and the world of generation and corruption. It begins, not with a discussion of the words 'in principio creavit', nor even with the Bible at all, but with a summary of the doctrines of 'the natural philosophers who discuss the nature of corruptible things'.

claims.text: Black says the frame of reference of the second exposition is the nature and function of the ten heavenly spheres, an ascent from the first exposition, in which 'heaven' is the empyrean and the eight lower spheres are 'earth'.

quotes.text: The transition from the first to the second exposition is an ascent from lower to higher. The frame of reference of the second exposition is the nature and function of the ten heavenly spheres.

In this context, applied to the Genesis account, 'heaven' is the empyrean, and the entire group of eight lower spheres (from the fixed stars down to, and including, the moon) are represented by the term 'earth'.

claims.text: In the second exposition Pico invokes his first-proem principle that Moses must not be made to look as if he had left anything out, to explain why four planets go unmentioned.

quotes.text: This leaves four planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter) so far unaccounted for. Pico had established a principle in the first proem that Moses should not be made to look as if he had left anything out. This principle is invoked here.

claims.text: Black says Pico credits an unnamed 'ancient Hebrew' doctrine, held to be a deeper mystery, that Jupiter and Mars are included in the sun and Venus and Mercury in the moon; the Hebrews give no reasons, so Pico supplies reason himself.

quotes.text: I believe that a deeper mystery of the ancient doctrine of the Jews lies hidden there. Among their beliefs about the heavens, this one is pre
eminent: that Jupiter and Mars are included by the sun, and Venus and Mercury by the moon.

These 'ancient Hebrews' are not named: it is, after all, a 'mystery', and as Pico remarked in the first proem things which are not hidden are not mysteries. Although they themselves do not give reasons for their doctrine, ratio will shine a light on the obscurity which they have left behind them.

judged.justification: Shows Pico attributing doctrine to unnamed Hebrew authorities and justifying it by reason.

claims.text: Pico says that whether one follows the authority of Aristotle, Avicenna or Averroes on celestial influence, their words, correctly interpreted, accord with those of Moses.

quotes.text: Pico passes over doctrinal disputes on this matter; regardless of whether one follows the authority of Aristotle, Avicenna or Averroes, their words (correctly interpreted) are in accord with the words of Moses.

claims.text: Black reports that the second exposition ends with Pico's warning that our souls, on the authority of Plato and unnamed theologians, were mixed in the same bowl as the heavenly bodies, so we should not fear, love and honour them rather than Christ.

quotes.text: The exposition ends with a warning by Pico that we should not regard ourselves as lower than the heavenly bodies, for, on the authority of Plato and unnamed theologians, our souls were mixed in the same bowl as them; nor should we fear, love and honour them rather than Christ.

claims.text: Black says that in the Third Exposition Pico had initially intended two expositions of the angelic world, one on Jewish teaching and one on Pseudo-Dionysius, but for lack of space and time concentrates on Dionysius alone, planning another book on the Jewish doctrine in which he will separate what accords with Catholic faith from what does not.

quotes.text: From consideration of the celestial spheres Pico ascends to contemplation of the intellectual world above them. He had initially intended to provide two expositions of the angelic world, one based on the teachings of the Jews, the other on Pseudo-Dionysius, but for reasons of space and time has decided to concentrate on the latter alone. He plans to devote another book to the Jewish doctrine, in which he will sift those elements of their teaching which are in accordance with the Catholic faith from those which are not. The third exposition will therefore concentrate on Dionysius.

judged.justification: Explains that the Heptaplus gives only the Dionysian plan of angels and postpones the Hebrew plan to a further book.

claims.text: Black notes that Pico says he follows the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather of Paul and Hierotheus whom Dionysius followed, and that the existence of Hierotheus, whom Pseudo-Dionysius calls his teacher, has been doubted.

quotes.text: Interea, Dionysii vestigiis insistentes, aut Pauli potius et Hierothei, quos ille est sequutus, conabimur tenebris legis
Pseudo-Dionysius refers to his 'teacher', Hierotheus, on several occasions, although the existence of this person has been doubted.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black in a footnote.

quote.text: Interea, Dionysii vestigiis insistentes, aut Pauli potius et Hierothei, quos ille est sequutus, conabimur tenebris legis

basis_quote.text: the existence of this person has been doubted

claims.text: Black says the third exposition begins by analysing the relationship of unity and number, applied to God and creation as a Pythagorean technique, and holds that as number depends on unity so angels depend on God.

quotes.text: The exposition begins with an analysis of the relationship between unitas and numerus. The latter is dependent on the former; the former depends only on itself. This philosophy of number is then applied to the relationship between God and creation, which, Pico says, is a Pythagorean technique. For unity 'which is from nothing, from which all things are' he substitutes God. Just as numerus depends on unitas, angels depend on God.

judged.justification: The number-unity model is the key to Pico's definition of angels as number.

claims.text: Black identifies the third exposition as treating angels as numbers: an angel is not unity itself, for it would then be God, so it must be number.

quotes.text: this identification of angels and numbers help to define the nature of the former?

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black: the angel is not unity itself, so it is number.

quote.text: Igitur angelus non est ipsa unitas, alioquin Deus esset, aut plures essent Dei, quod concipi ne potest quidem.

judged.justification: Makes the angel-number identification the hinge of the exposition.

claims.text: Black says Pico defines every number as imperfect as a multiplicity and perfect as a unity, and uses this interplay of perfection through participation in unity and imperfection through multiplicity as the definition of the nature of angels in general.

quotes.text: 'Every number,' he says, 'is imperfect insofar as it is a multiplicity, but perfect insofar as it is unity.' This interplay between perfection (through participation in unity) and imperfection (through multiplicity) is used as the definition of the nature of angels in general.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black.

quote.text: Est autem omnis numerus eatenus imperfectus quatenus multitudo, perfectus autem quatenus unus.

claims.text: Black states that an angel is imperfect in two respects: in essence, since it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and in cognition, since it is not intellection itself but understanding happens to it.

quotes.text: An angel is imperfect in two aspects. Regarding 'essence', it is not 'being itself', but only 'an essence to which being comes by participation, so that it may be'. Regarding cognition, it is not, in itself, intellectio, but 'it happens to it that it understands'.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black.

quote.text: Imperfectionem in angelo duplicem invenimus: alteram, quia non est ipsum esse, sed essentia tantum cui participatu esse accidit ut sit

judged.justification: States that in the Heptaplus the angel's being is participated, not identical with its essence.

claims.text: Black reads the first day in the third exposition as the drama of the angel overcoming its double imperfection: earth is its rough, unformed essence and heaven the acting of its essence and participation of unity in multiplicity, that is its connection to ipsum esse.

quotes.text: Pico's reading of the first day, spread over chapters one and two, concerns the drama of the angel overcoming this double imperfection. Chapter one deals with the question of its essence. Earth refers to the angel's 'rough and unformed essence, deprived of life and being'. Heaven is the 'acting of its essence and the participation of unity in multiplicity', in other words, its connection to ipsum esse.

claims.text: Black explains that in the third exposition the angel has an intellectual capacity but must be given intelligible forms, represented by light, which are accidents of its intellect and not part of its essence.

quotes.text: Chapter two turns to its cognition. The angel has an intellectual capacity but needs to be given intelligible forms to fulfil its function of contemplation. The absence of such forms is expressed by the shadows on the face of the abyss the abyss being the angel's
intellect. These intelligible forms are represented by light; they are accidents of the angel's intellect and do not pertain to its essence.

claims.text: Black reports that Pico's exegesis of 'one day' says the bond between forms and the angelic mind is stronger than that between forms and the human intellect, citing Averroes and Maimonides for the point and adding his own reason that the forms are joined to the angelic mind indivisibly.

quotes.text: Nonetheless, the bond which links these forms to the angelic intellect is stronger than the equivalent bond between forms and the human intellect. This is made clear in the exegesis of the conjunction of morning and evening which makes 'one day' (Genesis 1.5):

There was from evening and morning one day, because, as Averroes proved, from the intellect and the intelligible is made a greater 'one' than from matter and form; because, as he himself affirms and as Maimonides also writes, the truth is perceived far more in angels than in men.

judged.justification: Shows Averroes and Maimonides supporting the angelic knowledge doctrine.

claims.text: Black says Pico follows Pseudo-Dionysius in dividing the angelic hierarchy into three groups, which he represents by the two groups of waters and the firmament.

quotes.text: Once these matters have been dealt with, the simpler question of the division of the angels into ranks is approached. Pico follows Pseudo-Dionysius by dividing the angelic hierarchy into three groups; he represents these by the two groups of waters and the firmament.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black: the three hierarchies agree with Dionysius's teaching.

quote.text: Legimus autem positum firmamentum in medio aquarum, ubi tres nobis angelicae hierarchiae

judged.justification: Records that the threefold Dionysian hierarchy is mapped onto the waters and firmament.

claims.text: In Black's outline the lowest angelic group assists man, the middle group administers the celestial spheres, and the highest is engaged only in contemplation; the final chapter says Christ, though a man, was superior to the angels.

quotes.text: The lowest of these groups of angels have one goal, which is to assist man.

The middle group are charged with the administration of the celestial spheres, while the highest group are engaged only in contemplation. The final chapter addresses the question of the relationship of angels to humans, and states that Christ, though a man, was superior to the angels.

claims.text: Black points to Proclus's Elements of Theology, Proposition 1, for the idea that every number participates unity.

quotes.text: On the idea that every number 'participates unity', see Proclus, Elements of Theology, ed. and tr. E.R. Dodds (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1933, repr. 1964), 2-3 (Proposition 1).

judged.justification: Ties the number-unity model of angels to a Proclean proposition.

claims.text: Black notes that another Dionysian discussion of the dependency of all creation on God, in De caelesti hierarchia, comes immediately before the discussion of the angelic hierarchies.

quotes.text: Another discussion of the dependency of all creation on God is found in Pseudo-Dionysius, Corpus Dionysiacum, II, ed. G. Heil and A.M. Ritter (Berlin: De Gruyter, 1991), 20 (De caelesti hierarchia, 177B), immediately preceding the discussion of the hierarchies of angels.

claims.text: The Fourth Exposition begins by asserting that every detail of the creation narrative related to the three worlds can also be read as referring to man himself.

quotes.text: The fourth exposition begins with the assertion that all the details in the creation narrative which Pico has so far related to the three worlds can also be interpreted as referring to man himself.

claims.text: Black reports that in the fourth exposition, above the rational soul lies 'intelligence', shared with angels, and below it a 'sensual part' shared with animals.

quotes.text: of man are introduced, corresponding to the two groups of waters. Below the rational soul there is a 'sensual part', which is shared with animals; above the rational soul, there is 'intelligence', which is shared with angels.

claims.text: Black says the Spirit of God moving over the upper waters is identified in the fourth exposition with a greater and more divine intellect that illuminates the human intellect; Pico leaves open whether this is God or a mind close and akin to man.

quotes.text: The Spirit of God, which moves over the upper waters, is identified with 'a greater and more divine intellect' which illuminates the human intellect.

Intellectum enim, qui est in nobis, illustrat maior atque adeo divinus intellectus sive sit Deus (ut quidam volunt), sive proxima homini et cognata mens, ut fere omnes Graeci, ut Arabes, ut Hebraeorum plurimi volunt.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black in a footnote.

quote.text: Intellectum enim, qui est in nobis, illustrat maior atque adeo divinus intellectus sive sit Deus (ut quidam volunt), sive proxima homini et cognata mens

judged.justification: Pico leaves open whether the illuminating intellect is God or a created mind.

claims.text: Black says that in the fourth chapter of the Fourth Exposition Pico refers to a great controversy with unnamed recent philosophers, denying that sun and moon stand for the actual and potential intellect, and takes them to name two aspects of the one human intellect, turned up toward the greater intellect or down toward the sensual powers.

quotes.text: In the fourth chapter Pico discusses 'rational nature' in more detail. Referring obscurely to a 'great controversy' between himself and certain unnamed 'recent philosophers', he denies the possibility that the sun represents the 'intellect which is in actuality', and the moon, the 'potential intellect'. Rather, he takes the two appellations to refer to a double aspect of the one human intellect: it can either turn upwards, towards the 'greater intellect' (previously identified
with the 'Spiritus Domini'), or downwards, towards the 'sensual powers'.

open_questions.text: Who the unnamed recent philosophers were is not stated here.

claims.text: Black says that at the start of the fifth exposition Pico dedicates the first day's section to the angelic world and the other parts to the other worlds in succession, and that the first four expositions gave self-contained bodies of knowledge whereas the fifth turns to the vertical hierarchy of the cosmos as a whole, the golden chain of Homer.

quotes.text: At the outset of the fifth exposition, Pico writes that he will now dedicate the first 'particula' (in other words, the section concerned with the account of the first day) to the first world (that is, the angelic) and the other parts to the other worlds, in succession. The first four expositions presented self-contained bodies of knowledge drawn from the three worlds and man and including physics, astronomy, metaphysics and psychology.
In other words, he will now focus on the vertical hierarchy of the cosmos as a whole.

In the fifth exposition Pico promises to observe, in Moses's words, 'that golden chain of Homer, the rings of Plato hanging from the living power of the fabricator, as if from the true stone of the unconquered Hercules'.

judged.justification: Explains how expositions 1-4 differ in kind from 5-6: subject-matter blocks versus the chain of being.

claims.text: Black reports that the Fifth Exposition opens with angelic cognition, holding that the angelic nature is pure intellect, that minds are like eyes, and that angelic cognition involves some combination of actuality and potentiality represented by heaven and earth.

quotes.text: The fifth exposition opens with an account of angelic cognition. The comparison of the eye and the mind serves as an example of the correspondences inherent in the cosmos: 'To talk about the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, let us first consider that minds are somehow like eyes'
precise details of angelic cognition are not entirely agreed on, but that it somehow involves a combination of actuality and potentiality.
These two aspects are represented in the Genesis narrative by heaven and earth respectively.

judged.justification: Pico calls the angelic nature pure intellect while allowing potentiality in its cognition.

claims.text: Black says the whole sixth chapter of the fifth exposition is reminiscent of the Oratio, noting especially the placing of man at the midpoint of the world and the Hermetic citation.

quotes.text: the dignity of man. The entirety of the sixth chapter is reminiscent of the Oratio.
Among verbal and thematic echoes, note especially the placing of man in the
midpoint of the world (H. 5.6; Garin, 300-302. Oratio; Garin, 104) and the Hermetic citation

judged.justification: Connects the Heptaplus's account of man to the Oration.

claims.text: Pico argues that man's likeness to God cannot rest on the action of mind, because in that respect angels have a closer affinity to God than man does.

quotes.text: Firstly, he rejects the notion that God and man share physical form; secondly, he argues that their similarity cannot be predicated on the action of mind, since in this sense there is a closer affinity between angels and God than between man and God.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black: the traits of mind are the more excellent in angels and closer to the divine nature.

quote.text: Verum agnoscemus haec eadem, quanto in angelis sunt quam in nobis et potiora et contrariae minus naturae admixta, tanto cum divina natura plus similitudinis et cognationis habentia.

judged.justification: Pico ranks angels above man in likeness to God by mind while claiming a different unique affinity for man.

claims.text: Black says Pico locates the unique affinity of man and God in the way man's substance itself holds the substances of all natures, unlike angels and other intelligent creatures, which contain things only accidentally by knowing them.

quotes.text: Instead, he concludes that the unique affinity between man and God derives from the way in which man's 'substance' has bound up within it, in itself ('re ipsa') 'the substances of all natures and the fullness of the entire universe'. By 'in itself' he means to distinguish this essential quality of man from the accidental way in which angels and other intelligent creatures can be said to 'contain' things when they manage to 'know' them.

judged.justification: Contrasts the angelic containment of things by knowing with man's containment by nature.

claims.text: Black says God contains all things as their principium and in better quality than in themselves, while man contains them as their medium, holding higher things in an inferior quality and lower things in a superior one.

quotes.text: The difference in how they do this is that God contains all things through being their principium, man through being their medium; God contains all things but of better quality than they are in themselves, whereas man contains
things that are higher on the chain of being than himself in an inferior quality, and things that are lower on it than he is, in a superior one.

claims.text: In the seventh chapter of the fifth exposition, Black says, man's moral behaviour is held to affect the cosmos as a whole, which with God will avenge itself on him if he neglects his obligations.

quotes.text: The moral behaviour of man, therefore, has an effect on the cosmos as a whole, and the cosmos, together with God, will revenge itself upon him if he does not fulfil his obligations.

claims.text: Black observes that the Sixth Exposition has two readings of the Genesis narrative and suggests a threefold division of the Heptaplus into the first five expositions, the sixth and the seventh, which takes its cue from Pico's understanding of the Trinity.

quotes.text: The sixth exposition comprises two separate readings of the Genesis narrative: the first running from chapters one to four, and the second from chapters five to seven. It also suggests another way of looking at the structure of the Heptaplus, which is to divide it into three sections: the first five expositions, the sixth exposition and the seventh exposition. This structural division of the text takes its cue from Pico's understanding of the Trinity, the definition of which

judged.justification: Gives a second architecture of the Heptaplus, a triad of 5+1+1, alongside the seven.

claims.text: Black reports that the Sixth Exposition opens by defining God as unity divided into three, and finds three aspects of unity in each created thing: with itself, with another, and with its maker; these are mirrored in the structure of the Heptaplus, with expositions one to five, six and seven presenting them in turn.

quotes.text: constitutes the opening sentence of the sixth exposition: 'God is unity, divided into three in such a way that he does not depart from the simplicity of unity.' There are, says Pico, many traces of the Trinity in creation, but he intends to concentrate on just one, which has not previously been discussed by anyone. This is the fact that each created thing has three different aspects of unity:

These three aspects of unity are reflected in the structure of the Heptaplus, insofar as the first five expositions present the first aspect, the sixth presents the second aspect and the seventh presents the third aspect.

judged.justification: Ties the architecture of the work to a Trinitarian doctrine of unity, the theme of the One in Pico.

claims.text: Black says the sixth exposition is built on the notion of 'copulare', the first part concerning knowledge and the second morality, a connection he takes up in Chapter 6.

quotes.text: The last sentence explains the rationale underlying the double nature of this exposition. The two interpretations each revolve around the notion of 'copulare'. The former aspect concerns knowledge; the latter, morality.

claims.text: Black notes that the first part of the sixth exposition sets out a universal taxonomy of relationships between entities, at most fifteen according to Pico, and that Pico stretches the Genesis text, which never mentions bodies, to fit his allegorical reading.

quotes.text: The first of these two parts of the exposition presents a universal taxonomy of logical and formal relationships between entities. According to 'all the teachings of the philosophers', there are no more than fifteen such relationships.
There is no mention of 'corpora' in the Genesis narrative, at this point or any other. Pico is stretching the text to enable his allegorical reading.

claims.text: Black reports that in the sixth chapter of the sixth exposition Pico alludes to a deeper mystery: the eventual union of the part of intellectual light in us with the first mind, where all understanding is complete.

quotes.text: He then alludes to a 'deeper mystery': the eventual ('aliquando')
union of 'that part of intellectual light which is in us' with 'the first mind, where there is the plenitude and totality of all understanding'.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black.

quote.text: ipsi primo omnium intellectui primaeque menti, ubi plenitudo, ubi universitas omnis intelligentiae, aliquando coniungatur

judged.justification: Union with the first mind is a goal for the intellect in the Heptaplus.

claims.text: Black says that in the seventh chapter of the Sixth Exposition union with God is possible only through Christ, the mean who unites man and God, which binds the two halves of the exposition together.

quotes.text: Finally, in the seventh chapter, he turns to union with God himself, which is only to be accomplished through the intercession of Christ. This last point serves to bind the two halves of the sixth exposition together. Christ is identified as the last of the 'modi coniunctionis' enumerated in the first half: the mean.
It is Christ alone who combines man and God; therefore he alone can unite them.

claims.text: Black says the Seventh Exposition distinguishes natural felicitas, in which something attains God in itself, from supernatural felicitas, in which it attains God in Himself.

quotes.text: The seventh exposition is concerned with felicitas. The proem starts by distinguishing two sorts, 'natural' and 'supernatural'. It goes on to discuss the relationship between them. Natural felicitas is when something attains God in itself; supernatural, when it attains God in Himself.

claims.text: Black reports that Pico says no philosophical school takes man back to his beginning or end, which only theology offers; a footnote quotes Pico grouping several philosophers who place our reason in the intellect in act or in a higher one akin to us.

quotes.text: This, in turn, has an adverse effect on the dignity of man, as 'philosophers' have conceived of it. Although most schools of philosophy allow man some form of attainment of truth, none of them grants him a complete return 'to his beginning or end', which only theology can offer.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black in a footnote.

quote.text: Dare aliquid plus visi Avicenna, Averrois, Abubacher, Alexander et Platonici, nostram rationem in intellectu, qui actu est, aut aliquo superiore, nobis tamen cognato, quasi in suo fine firmantes, sed neque hi hominem ad suum principium nec ad suum finem adducunt.

judged.justification: Places Avicenna, Averroes, Alexander and the Platonists together as falling short of the full return.

claims.text: Black says that in the seventh exposition the capacity for supernatural felicitas is limited to man and angels, and neither can reach it without the help of Christ.

quotes.text: This capacity is limited to man and the angels; neither man nor angel can progress to this level without the help of Christ.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black in a footnote.

quote.text: Ad hanc angeli attolli quidem possunt, sed non possunt ascendere.

judged.justification: Angels are lifted to supernatural felicitas but cannot ascend to it, on Black's quotation of Pico.

claims.text: Black says the Seventh Exposition presents the progress to supernatural felicitas as a journey of all humanity through sacred history, its central fourth chapter arguing from Jewish sources that Christ is the Messiah.

quotes.text: Within the remainder of the seventh exposition, however, the progression to supernatural felicitas is presented not in terms of a single individual's attainment but in terms of the whole of humanity. It is articulated as a journey through sacred history.
The central chapter of this exposition, the fourth, is taken up with the demonstration that Christ is the Messiah, based on a polemical reading of Jewish sources.

claims.text: Black says the final section of the Heptaplus returns to the word bereshit and abandons allegory for a technique of letter combination derived from kabbalistic exegetical works, producing a sentence that summarises the Heptaplus and confirms Pico's claim that everything can be found in Moses's text.

quotes.text: At this point the main body of the Heptaplus is complete. There follows, however, a final section in which Pico returns to the first word of the Bible bereshit in Hebrew which he has until now neglected. He also turns away from the allegorical method which he has applied to the preceding seven expositions to 'another method of interpretation'.

For now, it must suffice to say that he adopts a technique of letter combination, derived from his reading of kabbalistic exegetical works, and uses it to construct a series of words from the single term bereshit. These words, put in order, produce a sentence which summarizes the Heptaplus as a whole. It is therefore further confirmation of his initial claim that everything can be discovered in Moses's text.

judged.justification: Sets the closing chapter as kabbalistic letter-technique, the frame within which the seven expositions are summarised.

claims.text: Black concludes that the Heptaplus is an array of allegorical identifications between things in the Genesis account and things or concepts in various philosophical disciplines, the choice of disciplines fixed by the three-world model, and built from previous example (auctoritas) or ratio, meaning analogies of structure.

quotes.text: As we have seen throughout this chapter, the Heptaplus consists of an array of allegorical identifications between things mentioned in the Genesis account and things or concepts in a variety of philosophical disciplines. The selection of disciplines is broadly determined by Pico's cosmic model of three interlinked worlds, which will be dis

cussed in Chapter 5. The allegorical identifications are constructed generally from previous example (auctoritas) or from ratio. By ratio Pico refers to patterns of similarity or analogy between the structure of the entities intrinsic to the Genesis account (heaven, earth, waters, etc.) and the structure of the entities or concepts extrinsic to it (causes, celestial spheres, relationship between body and soul etc.).

judged.justification: States the architecture in one place: the constant subject (Genesis), changing frameworks (disciplines), allegory by authority or analogy.

claims.text: Black distinguishes the Heptaplus's practice of allegorical reading from its theory of allegory, the relation of which to the work's form and content and to other theories is his subject of study.

quotes.text: Distinct from this practice of allegorical reading, however, the Heptaplus also contains a theory of allegory. This theory, the way in which it relates to the work's form and content, and the way in which it relates to other theories of biblical allegory, is my subject of study.

claims.text: Black says Pico tells his audience that his work is unprecedented and not derived from previous commentators, thereby framing the Heptaplus in opposition to preceding commentary traditions.

quotes.text: Pico tells his audience that his work is unprecedented and that he has not derived his interpretations from previous commentators. In other words, he frames the Heptaplus in opposition to the various commentary traditions which preceded it.

claims.text: Black says the medieval fourfold method of literal, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses remained dominant in the fifteenth century, and that Pico himself in the Apologia recognised it as the normal Christian way of reading the Bible.

quotes.text: One is the medieval tradition of the four senses of Scripture, which, I argue, maintained its place as the dominant hermeneutic model
the literal or historical, the allegorical, the moral or tropological and the anagogical. Pico himself, in the Apologia, recognized that this was the normal Christian way of interpreting the Bible.

claims.text: Black observes that Nicholas of Lyra's stricter definition of the spiritual senses was copied almost verbatim from Aquinas at the start of the Summa theologiae, which the quoted passage grounds partly in Dionysius on the new law as figure of future glory.

quotes.text: Nor did the stricter definition given in the Postilla originate from the pen of Nicholas of Lyra: he copied, almost
verbatim, the discussion of the same matter given by Thomas Aquinas at the beginning of the Summa theologiae.
ut dicit Dionysius in Ecclesiastica Hierarchia, est figura futurae gloriae

warrants.text: Aquinas's Latin as quoted by Black cites Dionysius in the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy for the new law as figure of future glory.

quote.text: ut dicit Dionysius in Ecclesiastica Hierarchia, est figura futurae gloriae

claims.text: Black says Pico's phrase 'apud nos' comes in his defence of kabbalah in the Apologia, where he argues that the Jews have a fourfold scheme parallel to the Christian one, with Pesat, Midras, Sechel and Cabala as the literal, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses.

quotes.text: This, then, was what Pico was referring to when he mentioned the interpretative method 'apud nos'. The context in which he makes this comment is his defence of kabbalah in the Apologia. One of the elements of this defence was to point out that the Jews, too, had a fourfold scheme of reading parallel to that of the Christians and that kabbalah fitted into the Jewish scheme in the same way that anagogy fitted into the Christian one. The Jewish scheme, Pico says, is 'Pesat' for the literal meaning, 'Midras' for the allegorical, 'Sechel' for the tropological and 'Cabala' for the anagogical.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black: Cabala is the anagogic sense, taught orally to Moses, lifting from the sensible to the intelligible.

quote.text: Anagogicus dicitur Cabala, et hoc quia illa expositio quae dicitur ore Dei tradita Moysi, et accepta per successionem, modo praedicto, quasi semper sensum sequitur Anagogicum

judged.justification: Shows kabbalah presented as the Jewish equivalent of anagogy.

claims.text: Black argues that aligning the fourfold methods of the two traditions was meant to make kabbalah less alien to Christian readers, so that Pico's argument depends on readers taking the fourfold method as the norm.

quotes.text: two traditions was intended to make kabbalah appear less alien to Christian readers by inserting it into a recognizable framework; as such, Pico's argument depends on the reader perceiving the fourfold method as the norm.

claims.text: Black thinks Pico's Apologia matching of terms to senses contains a mistake, since Sechel as practised by Gersonides, Maimonides and Ibn Ezra would more accurately be the allegorical and Midras the tropological, perhaps from haste in writing the Apologia.

quotes.text: There seems to be a mistake in Pico's attributions here. 'Sechel' as practised by Gersonides, Maimonides and Abraham ibn Ezra he equates with the tropological method whereas it would more accurately be the allegorical; and 'midras', which he equates with the allegorical, should rather be the tropological.
The mistake here may merely be due to Pico's haste in writing the Apologia.

claims.text: Black notes that the survey of incunable biblical commentary shows no printed commentaries solely and specifically on Genesis, though Genesis commentaries may have existed in manuscript.

quotes.text: There appear to be no printed commentaries solely and specifically on Genesis.
This is not to assert, of course, that other general works, and works specifically on Genesis, were not available in manuscript

claims.text: Black sums up that the survey presents the norms for biblical interpretation in the late fifteenth century, against which Pico's own comment on which authors bear on the Genesis narrative is largely antithetical.

quotes.text: This survey of texts and methods presents the norms for biblical interpretation in the late fifteenth century. A largely antithetical perspective is to be found in Pico's own comment regarding which authors he considered to be of relevance to an analysis of the Genesis narrative.

judged.justification: Frames the Heptaplus's authorities as deliberately unlike the fifteenth-century norm.

claims.text: Black says that in the first proem Pico, to substantiate the claim that his method is new, lists authorities he will not imitate, and that this list shows what Pico himself regarded as significant in biblical commentary.

quotes.text: Before telling his readers what the Heptaplus is, Pico informs them of what it is not. He claims that his method of interpretation is new. To substantiate this claim, he gives a list of authorities 'robust minds' in the field of biblical commentary whose work he will not imitate and whose methods he will not follow.
Let us rather, beyond all these, contribute seven other expositions, the product of our own invention and reflection.

judged.justification: Treats the first-proem list as evidence of what Pico knew, not only as rhetoric.

claims.text: Black says the Heptaplus is explicitly defined by its author against a background of exegesis in four languages and two faiths, stretching from well-known Latin exegetes into an uncertain twilight of Greek and Hebrew figures unrepresentative of fifteenth-century Christian commentary.

quotes.text: The Heptaplus, then, is explicitly defined by its author against a background of exegesis drawn from four languages and two faiths. This background extends from several of the fundamental and well-known Latin exegetes mentioned above into a vague and uncertain twilight of Greek and Hebrew figures who were certainly not representative of Christian biblical commentary in the fifteenth century.

claims.text: Black identifies Pico's listed exegetes guided by Pico's phrase 'super hoc libro', meaning works specifically on Genesis, and by Pico's library inventories and other collections, noting that Pico's own access to the Vatican appears to have ended in March 1487.

quotes.text: answering this it is necessary to identify those who are referred to ambiguously. I have generally been guided in this attempt by Pico's own comment, that these are the authors who have previously produced significant work 'super hoc libro', that is, specifically on Genesis. It is also necessary to consider to what extent the works of these authors were available to Pico. In this respect we have the good fortune to possess his library inventories and my analysis is largely based on these.
Pico's own access to the Vatican appears to have ended in March 1487, however.

claims.text: Black notes that both Albertus and Aegidius figure in the Conclusiones, Aegidius with eleven conclusions and Albertus with sixteen.

quotes.text: Both Albertus and Aegidius figure in Pico's Conclusiones, Aegidius with eleven conclusions and Albertus with sixteen.

claims.text: Black says Pico was particularly interested in Origen, whose orthodoxy Pico defends in the Apologia, and that Origen's work on Genesis probably reached him in the Latin translation of Rufinus.

quotes.text: Pico was particularly interested in Origen
See his defence of Origen's orthodoxy in the Apologia, in Opera omnia, 199-224
were therefore only extant, aside from a few excerpts in the catena tradition, in the Latin translation of Rufinus, made around 400 AD.
The manuscript circulation of this work was wide and it was presumably the main source of Pico's knowledge of Origen's Genesis exegesis.

bears_on.note: Pico's Apologia defended Origen's orthodoxy.

claims.text: Black argues that Pico's only access to Didymus's lost Genesis commentary must have been through the Genesis catena, and that Pico's mention of an author, as with Didymus, does not imply that the author's works were directly available to him.

quotes.text: Pico's only access to this material must therefore have been through the catena, several manuscripts of which were to be found in the Vatican.
As in the case of Didymus, Pico's mention of an author does not imply that his works were directly available to him.

judged.justification: Warns that Pico's lists of authorities can be second-hand names.
