claims.text: Black proposes that Pico's 'Eusebius' is Eusebius of Emesa because the works by another Eusebius in Pico's library contain no interpretation of Genesis whereas Emesa's commentary on the Octateuch was among the most cited in the Genesis catena.

quotes.text: None of these is an interpretation of Genesis, however, which leads me to propose that 'Eusebius' in fact refers to Eusebius of Emesa (c. 300-c. 359) whose commentary on the Octateuch, although not extant in direct transmission, was one of the most widely cited works in the Genesis catena.

claims.text: Black leaves open which of two authors Pico's 'Theodoretus' means, since the catena labels excerpts from 'Theodorus' variously.

quotes.text: In any case, excerpts from this 'Theodorus' are sometimes labelled in the catena as coming from 'Theodoretus' or simply the abbreviated 'Theod.'. Which of these two authors this name refers to, then, must remain an open question; both were a part of the Antiochene school.

open_questions.text: Which Theodore Pico means is unresolved.

basis_quote.text: Which of these two authors this name refers to, then, must remain an open question

claims.text: Black concludes, leaving some names unresolved, that many of Pico's listed authors may have reached him only as names and fragments, and that the catena played a decisive role in forming his list whether or not it played any role in his actual exegesis.

quotes.text: These questions must remain unanswered; it is not my intention to pursue a holy grail of positive attribution when the evidence suggests that many of these authors could have come down to Pico only as names and fragments. What this analysis does show is that the catena played a decisive role in the formation of his list, whether or not it played any role in his actual exegesis.

claims.hedge_words: could have come down to Pico only as names and fragments

open_questions.text: Identity of Severus and Josephus and whether the catena informed Pico's exegesis are unsettled.

claims.text: Black says Pico's 'Chaldeans' Anchelos and Ionethes are traditional names for two Aramaic Targumim, and that Pico possessed a 1482 Pentateuch containing the Targum Onkelos with the commentary of Rashi.

quotes.text: 'Chaldean' to Pico and his contemporaries meant Aramaic; the 'Chaldeans', 'Anchelos' and 'Ionethes', are the two names traditionally connected to two of the Targumim or Aramaic biblical translations.
Pico possessed an edition of the Pentateuch, published in 1482, which included the Targum Onkelos, as well as the commentary of Rashi.

claims.text: Black thinks it likely that Pico's 'Simeon' the Chaldean is Simeon bar Yohai, but says that what in fact lies behind the reference is the Zohar, attributed to him.

quotes.text: Given that 'Simeon', too, is a 'Chaldean', it is likely that Pico was referring to the Palestinian Simeon bar Yo .hai
but, in fact, what lies behind this reference is the Zohar, written in Aramaic in the thirteenth century and attributed to Simeon bar Yo .hai.

judged.justification: Identifies the Zohar behind a name in the first proem.

claims.text: Black says Pico knew of the Zohar but named it only once and there is no evidence he had the work itself; his knowledge appears to have come from intermediaries, notably Recanati's Pentateuch commentary, which quotes it extensively.

quotes.text: Pico knew of the Zohar, but he refers to it by name only once and we have no evidence that the work itself was available to him.
His knowledge of it appears to have been gained from intermediary sources, notably the commentary on the Pentateuch of Menahem Recanati, which quotes the Zohar (in Aramaic) extensively.

judged.justification: Corrects any assumption that Pico read the Zohar directly.

claims.text: Black says Pico regarded Maimonides as a kabbalist, being particularly influenced by Abulafia's commentary on the Guide (Sitrei Torah), which Mithridates translated as De secretis legis and which played a formative role in Pico's conception of kabbalah.

quotes.text: Pico regarded Maimonides as a kabbalist. He was particularly influenced in this regard by the commentary on the Guide of Abraham Abulafia (1240-after 1291), entitled Sitrei Torah ('Secrets of the Torah'), which was translated for Pico by Mithridates under the title De secretis legis. This latter work played a formative role in Pico's conception of kabbalah.

warrants.text: Pico's Latin as quoted by Black: Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, in the Guide, embraces mysteries of the Cabala under a philosophical surface.

quote.text: Rabi Moyses Aegyptius in libro, qui a latinis dicitur Dux neutrorum, dum per superficialem verborum corticem videtur cum philosophia ambulare, per latentes profundi sensus intelligentias mysteria complectitur Cabalae.

bears_on.note: Mithridates translated Abulafia's commentary for Pico.

judged.justification: Names Abulafia as a formative source and Maimonides as read cabalistically.

claims.text: Black observes that the chapter headings of Abulafia's work include creation topics, suggesting Pico would have regarded it as a source on the Genesis narrative, and thinks it conceivable that Pico's 'Abraam' refers to Abulafia.

quotes.text: Its chapter headings include 'de principio et causa', 'de actu et potentia', 'de opere geneseos', 'de caelo et terra', 'de aquis superioribus' and 'de materia et forma', among others, which suggests that Pico would have considered it as a source of relevant information on the Genesis narrative. It is conceivable, then, that the 'Abraam' in the list refers to Abulafia.

claims.text: Black says Pico owned a printed Nahmanides Pentateuch commentary and mentions Nahmanides in the Apologia, the Psalms expositions and the Heptaplus, but the Heptaplus reference could have come from Recanati's quotation of him, so it is unclear how much Pico read Nahmanides.

quotes.text: Nahmanides wrote a well-known commentary on the Pentateuch, a printed edition of which was in Pico's library.

Pico mentions Nahmanides once in the Apologia and once in the Expositiones in Psalmos. He also cites him in the Heptaplus. Here, however, the reference could equally have come from Recanati's quotation of Nahmanides in his commentary on the Pentateuch. Pending further analysis, it is not yet clear to what extent Pico actually read Nahmanides.

open_questions.text: How far Pico read Nahmanides directly is unsettled.

basis_quote.text: it is not yet clear to what extent Pico actually read Nahmanides

claims.text: Black says Gersonides exercised an undeniable influence on Pico's concept of exegesis, seen in the Job manuscript and in Pico's annotated Mithridates translation of Gersonides on the Song of Songs, though it is unclear that Pico read Gersonides on the Pentateuch.

quotes.text: Levi ben Gershom (otherwise known as Gersonides), on the other hand, exercised an undeniable influence on Pico's concept of exegesis. In the first place, this is evident from Pico's Job manuscript, which bears the imprint of Gersonides's own commentary on Job. In the second place, Pico owned and annotated a translation made for him by Mithridates of Gersonides's commentary on the Song of Songs.
As with Nahmanides, however, it is not clear that Pico actually read Gersonides's commentary on the Pentateuch, although he did own a printed copy of it.

bears_on.note: Mithridates translated Gersonides on the Song of Songs for Pico.

judged.justification: Makes Gersonides an undeniable influence on Pico's concept of exegesis.

claims.text: Black says Recanati's Pentateuch commentary was Pico's principal point of entry to the Zohar, was translated for him by Mithridates in 1486, and was an influential source for his interpretation of kabbalah in the 900 Conclusiones.

quotes.text: 'Manaem' refers to Menahem Recanati, whose commentary on the Pentateuch, as noted above, was Pico's principal point of entry to the Zohar.

Mithridates at some point in 1486, but this version is largely no longer extant. Recanati's commentary on the Pentateuch was an influential source for Pico's interpretation of kabbalah in the 900 Conclusiones.

bears_on.note: Mithridates translated Recanati for Pico.

claims.text: Black sums up that the Hebrew exegetes in Pico's list are a cross-section of the best-known medieval Jewish exegetes, that Pico had access to their works though often only in Hebrew, and that the Psalm citations show he could draw on untranslated works such as Ibn Ezra and Rashi.

quotes.text: This group, in sum, represents an accurate cross-section of the most well-known and influential medieval Jewish exegetes. It is clear that Pico had access to their works, but in many cases he was limited to Hebrew texts. The citations in the Expositiones in Psalmos, discussed below, show that he was able to draw on some of these untranslated works, such as Ibn Ezra and Rashi.

claims.text: Black says 'Neonias' probably refers to Nehunya ben Ha-Kanah, to whom the Bahir was attributed; the Bahir opens with a quotation from him, Pico read it in Mithridates's version and used it in the Conclusiones.

quotes.text: It is harder to say what context lies behind the names of the 'ancient' commentators, Eleazarus, Aba, Ioannes, Neonias, Isaac and Ioseph. 'Neonias' probably refers to Nehunya ben Ha-Kanah, to whom the Sefer Bahir was sometimes attributed. The Bahir starts with a quotation from him, spelt (in Mithridates's translation) 'Nehonias'. Pico read the Bahir in this version and used it in the Conclusiones.

bears_on.note: Pico read the Bahir in Mithridates's translation.

claims.text: Black notes that the Bahir cites a Rabbi Johanan on Genesis 1, that Eleazar, Abba and Isaac are cited in the Zohar and so in Recanati, and that these names also occur in Bereshit Rabbah, of which Pico owned an untranslated copy; other sources may have existed.

quotes.text: The Bahir is essentially an exegetical work, and a fair proportion of its sections relate to the Genesis narrative. It is structured as a series of brief citations of ancient rabbis. Among these, we find a Rabbi Johanan, who comments on certain verses from Genesis 1

Rabbis by the name of Eleazar, Abba and Isaac are all cited regularly in the Zohar and hence in Recanati's commentary on the Pentateuch. These names, as well as Johanan, are also to be found in the Midrash on Genesis, Bereshit Rabbah, of which Pico owned an untranslated copy. There may well have been other such sources.

claims.hedge_words: There may well have been other such sources

claims.text: Black argues that one essential function of Pico's list of rejected authorities is to impress the reader with his acquaintance with a wide range of commentaries, and that formulating the list negatively doubles its rhetorical impact.

quotes.text: What can we conclude from this analysis? Clearly, one essential function of the list is to impress the reader. While not neglecting a representative sample of canonical works, it serves to emphasize Pico's acquaintance with a remarkably wide range of commentaries.

By formulating this list negatively, as comprising those authors whom he will not use, Pico doubles its rhetorical impact. The implication is that he was sufficiently learned not only to read these authors but also to proffer interpretations that they had missed.

judged.justification: Reads the list as rhetoric as well as evidence of reading.

claims.text: Black warns that knowing an author's name does not imply knowing the text: many 'ancient Hebrews' were known through intermediaries such as the Bahir and Recanati, and many early Greek exegetes through fragments in the catena.

quotes.text: Beyond this rhetorical level, however, the question of exactly what the list represents is not entirely clear-cut. Although, as we have seen, almost all the names can be connected either to works available to Pico or to figures mentioned in works available to him, knowledge of the name does not necessarily imply knowledge of the text.

Many of the 'ancient Hebrews', meanwhile, were known to him through citations in intermediary works such as the Bahir and Recanati's commentary on the Pentateuch. The same is true of a substantial proportion of the early Greek exegetes, who were not passed down in direct transmission but had survived only as fragments in the catena.

judged.justification: Qualifies claims of direct knowledge of Pico's cited authorities.

claims.text: Black concludes that despite these doubts the list shows Pico's frame of reference was broad compared with contemporary norms and his exegetical toolkit better stocked than most.

quotes.text: Despite the questions raised by this list, it shows that Pico's frame of reference was broad in comparison to contemporary norms and that his exegetical toolkit was better stocked than most.

claims.text: Black says the attention Pico gives to Genesis in the Heptaplus differs fundamentally from his other exegetical works; the Heptaplus relies on the Vulgate text of Genesis 1.1-27, whereas the Job manuscript and Psalms commentaries scrutinise translation.

quotes.text: Further examination will confirm that the attention which Pico pays to Genesis in the Heptaplus is of a fundamentally different nature from that of his other exegetical works.
The Heptaplus relies on the Vulgate, the relevant section of which (Genesis 1.1-27) is included at the end of the second proem.
By contrast, both Pico's Job manuscript and his Psalms commentaries display a marked scrutiny of scriptural translation.

judged.justification: Separates the Heptaplus from Pico's philological exegesis.

claims.text: Black reports that in a 1489 letter to Andrea Corneo Pico described a new work undertaken with the encouragement of Lorenzo de' Medici, to interpret the Psalms at length and to defend the Septuagint against the Jews.

quotes.text: This twofold intention is clear from his letter of 1489 to Andrea Corneo, in which he writes that he has in hand 'a new work, with the encouragement of Lorenzo de' Medici'. Firstly, he will 'illuminate, with a longish interpretation, the Psalms of David'. Secondly, he will defend the Septuagint version, which the Jews falsely claim departs from the Hebrew in over six hundred places.

bears_on.note: Lorenzo encouraged Pico's Psalms work in 1489.

claims.text: Black says the double aim of the Psalm expositions, interpretation and defence of a translation, was repeated at the beginning of the Heptaplus, showing that philology's purpose was polemical rather than merely scholarly.

quotes.text: summary of the double nature of the Expositiones in Psalmos was repeated at the beginning of the Heptaplus, revealing the practice and purpose of philology as Pico and his contemporaries saw it
philological analysis works by confronting different versions, and its purpose is polemical, not simply scholarly.

claims.text: Black concludes from soundings that Pico's philological sections compare four versions of the Psalms, give the Septuagint precedence and correct Hebrew exegetes by reference to textual transmission; defending the Septuagint also defends the standard Gallician Psalter, making Pico a more conservative philologist than Valla or Manetti.

quotes.text: These are no more than soundings, but they are enough to illustrate Pico's method. The philological sections of his Psalm commentaries proceed by comparing the four versions of the text

When the texts disagree, the Septuagint, in the examples above at least, is given precedence. The Hebrew exegetes are 'corrected' on this basis, with reference to common mistakes of textual transmission.
His defence of established Christian versions of the Bible makes Pico a more conservative philologist than Valla or Manetti.
in defending the Septuagint version of the Psalms, he is also defending the Gallician Psalter, which was translated from it.
